utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, all the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Stojic. For the Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're going to proceed and conclude the examination-in-chief, and then we'll have the first of the cross-examinations from Madame Fauveau, who represents General Miletic. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. Good afternoon, General. Just a couple more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned, I think at the very end of your testimony yesterday, about your observations of the relationship between the high Serb, Bosnian Serb, political and military leadership. In the aftermath of the Srebrenica and Zepa operations, and in particular in the aftermath of the VRS losses in the Grahovo-Glamoc front following the HVO offensive, did you become aware of any criticism directed at the Main Staff and General Mladic in particular?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory is there was some reaction in the Parliament, the Bosnian Serb Parliament, but beyond that I can't -- I don't have a very clear memory of any particular event other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The last area I'd like to discuss with you is, again just to be clear, going to be based on your personal experience and observations during your service in Bosnia. It's an area of your personal experience that you did refer to in your expert statement, but I want to emphasise again this is factual -- more factual testimony I'm going to be eliciting, and that is regarding the role and effect of propaganda and disinformation, as you saw it during that time. You refer to this in your expert statement at pages 18 and 26 to 27 of the English and pages 16 to 17 and 24 of the B/C/S. Now, I think they can typically be two distinct concepts, but I want to ask you some questions based on your experience there. And let's go directly to the expert statement itself, and I'll just read from it as well. We're at 6D00183, please, and that's again page 18 of the English and pages 16 to 17 of the B/C/S. We're just waiting for the B/C/S, General, and when we get there, the relevant portion of the B/C/S appears at my question to you about the middle of the page. Now, the Trial Chamber will hear from General Nicolai and others about various conversations between Generals Gvero and Tolimir during the VRS attack on Srebrenica, including the one that's referred to here in my question at the top of the page, on page 1 of the English, and I'm -- page 18 of the -- pardon me, page 18 of the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 16 of the B/C/S, if we could back up -- or go forward to page 18 of the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, this telephone call between Generals Gvero and Nicolai, we'll hear about later from General Nicolai himself, but I put the question to you: In your experience, the reference in this telephone call to Gvero telling General Nicolai that the Muslims were doing the firing during the attack on Srebrenica, I asked you if that was something you'd heard before, an example of anything in particular that you could comment on, and your answer is at lines 5 through 16. And then further down the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I submit this is a highly objectionable way of doing this. If my learned friend wants to ask this question as a fact-based exercise, then put the intercept in front of the witness, invite the witness to look at it, and then invite him to draw conclusions from it based on his own personal experience. But going to a document in this leading form, which is and was intended as an expert statement, still labelled as such, is not the way to go about it, bearing in mind the ruling of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to rephrase the question. I don't think there was any need at all to tell the witness that we will be hearing from General Nicolai himself on this, et cetera, et cetera. Just go straight to the document and put the questions you would like to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe, General, what the effect of these types of conversations that were being engaged in between Generals Gvero and Tolimir and Generals Gobillard, Nicolai and ultimately General Janvier had given the way that you had to operate in UNPROFOR and in conjunction with NATO? Can you just tell the Trial Chamber what effect this type of information had?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequence of receiving information like this, or the assertion such as this, is that a delay was introduced into the UN and, if necessary, the NATO decision-making process. There is a -- both parties were in the habit of blaming the other for various actions, but if you were there, standing in the middle, as we were in the UN, and you had fairly precise instructions as to what you could and couldn't do with the use of military force, then you had to be very clear as to who had done what. And the moment one of the parties was asserting that they hadn't done it, you found yourself in a position where you had to work your way through a process of verification of the information, and usually the moment of taking action had then passed by the time you'd done -- carried out that action -- carried out that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And perhaps it would be helpful to describe a little bit about the actual process that got delayed by having to verify this information. If you could get into perhaps the mechanics a little bit so that the Trial Chamber gets a clearer picture.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the use of NATO as -- for air attacks and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I don't know how much the -- has been explained about the dual key and the arrangements by which NATO air power could be used. However do you want me to explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It would probably be helpful to start towards the beginning. We haven't heard too much testimony here about that particular topic. We've certainly heard about close air support, a little bit about the air strikes, but not so much about the process. So you can --

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with the decisions to involve the NATO -- North Atlantic Treaty Organisation in these operations, you arrived at a situation where you had, leave aside the Bosnians, the Bosnian Serbs, the Federation and so on, you now had a United Nations force on the ground, with some aeroplanes, helicopters in the main, and a NATO air force in the air, each answering to different political groups or political direction; the Security Council, on the one hand, and the North Atlantic Council on the other. In order to make this work and key these two activities and organisations together, NATO arrived at a method of operating which came to be called "the dual key arrangement," in which both the NATO commander and the UN commander both had to agree that the -- that the air response was necessary. In other words, essentially three areas in which NATO got involved. The first was to police the no-fly zone, and here it was relatively easy to work. NATO informed -- I beg your pardon. The UN informed NATO of when it was flying its aeroplanes, and NATO then worked on the basis that everything else they saw flying wasn't the UN, and if they could identify it themselves as a violator of the no-fly zone, they shot it down, which they did on some occasions. Then there was the close air support of the UN forces in their self-defense. I talked yesterday of the need for the forward air controllers for this, but there was a -- this could be called upon by the UN, and provided it was absolutely clear that this was in self-defence of the UN, as a UN force, as opposed to any other use of air power for any other purpose, then the decisions could be made quite quickly. There were relatively few barriers to making the decision, and -- but nevertheless both UN and NATO had to turn their keys. Finally, there was a use of air power that starts with the imposition of the exclusion zones around the safe areas. This was intended to reduce the use of -- or neutralise the use of Bosnian Serb artillery and other heavy weapons in affecting the people living inside these safe areas. Here, provided the violation could be identified, then NATO could be called upon to attack it, but again both the UN and NATO commanders had to turn their keys, and the process of making that decision was slightly more involved, and as I think we've already -- I think I've already answer answered a question to this, during May the matter became highly political and, in fact, was taken out of the hands of UN the commanders and political officials in the theatre of operations itself. So the consequence of the entirely understandable reaction that, "I didn't do it, he did it," was that this delayed the process by which you could bring in that air power, which was already complex enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we look at 65 ter 2940A, please. And the correct B/C/S version will be 2940C.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, this is an intercept dated 10 July at 2015 hours, a conversation in which the participants have been identified as General Janvier and General Tolimir. If we could scroll down just a little bit on the English. Great, thank you. Just take a moment and read the intercept there in front of you. General Tolimir says: "I don't believe our soldiers are attacking your soldiers, since they have been avoiding it up to now." A few lines down, he says: "I will check now with the commander in that area. He hasn't reported to me that there was any attack." We need to scroll down a little bit, I think, on both versions. "I will personally check the information you gave me by phone." "I will order my commander to establish, through UNPROFOR soldiers on our side, radio contact with your check-point, the one you said was attacked." We can go to the next page of the intercept. General Janvier says that the VRS has to stop and withdraw to where they were. And then General Tolimir says: "I'm going to check the situation. Call me back in 20 to 30 minutes, the time needed to establish contact and give the required orders." And then: "Okay, in 30 minutes we will call you again." In the context, General, of the ongoing attack on the enclave, in your experience, how important or not important was it to identify who, if anyone, was attacking UN troops or positions in respect to calling in for close air support? It may be an obvious question, but --

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: You couldn't bring -- you had to identify your attacker in order to counter-attack or defeat the attack. So for that reason, it was important to identify it. The -- and you would not get close air support unless you could give the pilot and the controllers a precise target. So it was important to establish it for those reasons, if for no other. You would also want to know which side you were about to attack, because your purpose was to get it to stop. So if you could get on the radio and say, "Stop --" you know, "I'm the one you're shooting at," then that would be an even better result than bringing in an air attack, if it stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. My name is Natacha Fauveau Ivanovic, and I respect General Miletic. I would like to ask you a few questions on the book that you wrote, "The Utility of Force." Is it true that in this book you wrote that military force, when it is used, has only two immediate effects; it kills people and it destructs things?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote that, yes. I think I used the word "destroy" rather than "destructs," but other than that, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, indeed, you used the term "destroy," yes. You also said that military combats are brutal because force is applied by armed military force, by lethal weapons?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You also developed an interesting theory about war waged among people, a new form of war which has developed over the last few years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've -- I have that argument in the book, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to read to you what you said on that particular war waged among people. This is on page 3 of your book, and in e-court this is Exhibit 5D516, page 9. I will read you this excerpt in English. It will be more accurate [in English]: "War among the people is different. It is the reality in which the people in the streets and houses and fields, all the people anywhere at the battlefield." [Interpretation] It is on the bottom of the page on the right-hand side. You did write this?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could it be said that recent wars, and civil wars in particular, and in particular the war waged in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the 1990s, is part of that particular category, i.e., a war waged among people?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is this true, that in these wars waged among people, war affects much more the civilian population than in traditional wars which were waged between armies on the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true. If we look at the casualties in the Second World War, there were very high numbers of civilians. The -- you should -- to understand my use of the "war amongst the people," you should read the whole of the paragraph you referred me to. It is -- I direct you to the top of the paragraph, where I say it is both a graphic description of modern war-like situations and a conceptual framework.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But would you agree that the civilian population is heavily affected in a war that could be called "a war among people"?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could one say that during that type of war, which is led everywhere, insecurity prevails?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the most general sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it be said that fear is a prevailing feeling in that type of wars?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any -- let us draw a distinction between the fight, the battle. In the battle, or the fight, or the engagement, fear, insecurity, are frequently felt emotions. That doesn't follow that those exist throughout a period of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But in the type of war that was waged in Bosnia, where the war was everywhere, as you rightly said in your book when you mention this concept of wars among people, can it be said that, generally speaking, the civilian population was scared?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all the time, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Indeed, but when there are combats close-by, or just before combats, or after combats, or when there's a shift in power, or when an army would enter into a city once the city fell, in those situations can we say that fear was a dominant feeling?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd be prepared to say that fear was a feeling. We'd have to ask each individual where it stood in their scheme of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In your testimony in the case against Dragomir Milosevic, you testified on the 7th of March, you spoke about military targets, and you said, and this is page 3351 of the transcript: [in English]: "The military target is the -- the significance of the military target is the military force, rather than specifically its locality. The military force might be using the locality to advantage, such as a hill with a church on it or whatever, and so it can then become a military target, but it is because the military are there, not because it exists as such." [Interpretation] Could we say that any building can become a military target if used by a military force, if this particular place is occupied by a military force?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think you can say that as precisely as you're asking me to answer the question, but you -- you would tend to that judgement, yes. But it gets harder and harder, the more important the building is, for whatever that reason -- whatever the reason for the importance of that building, a mosque, for example, or a church.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it be said that in wars among people, that is, the war waged in Bosnia, armed forces would commonly use civilian buildings and even sometimes humanitarian buildings for military operations?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, people did do that in the Bosnian example.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that at an inferior level of a military organisation, i.e., at the battalion level, for example, or sometimes even at the brigade level, simple houses were used as unit headquarters, and those military unit headquarters could not be distinguished from the neighbouring houses where simple people lived?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with the first part of your question, that, yes, civil houses were used for headquarters. I don't agree that you couldn't differentiate between the two. If you knew one was a headquarters, you must know where it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau, this last line of questions of yours, I think, are very generic. They seem to cover not only the whole territory scenario of the war, scene of the war, but also it doesn't have a time frame. If you could be more specific, I think it would be much better.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm reaching the end of that line of questions, anyway. Indeed, they were quite generic. If you allow me, I'd like to clarify the last answer given by the witness, because my question may not have been entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I meant is that military units would not indicate their headquarters very distinctively so they could be differentiated from other houses. Right?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no one's trying to make himself obvious on a battlefield, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the testimony you gave in August 1996, it is actually a statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, this is page 6, first paragraph, and this is Exhibit 6D180, in this statement you describe General Mladic. This is the very first paragraph. You said, among other things in this statement [in English]: ... "Resolute and remained rational and in control under pressure. I believe he was driven by a single overarching aim of the defence of the Bosnian Serbs and all else was to be subordinated to the achievement of this aim." [Interpretation] According to this description you gave of General Mladic, his one objective in this war was to defend the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding of him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I have one more generic question. I hope the Bench will allow me to put it. I promise it's the last one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that the aim of war, the most common -- the most traditional aim of war is the fact that people want to take control of territory?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that is the only or traditional aim of warfare.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it be said that it is or that it can be one of the aims pursued through war?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In July 1995, when you were commander of the UNPROFOR forces for Bosnia and Herzegovina, General Nicolai was your Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for six of those months of that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When General Nicolai was away from your HQ, for instance, when he went to Bratunac to attend the departure of the Dutch Battalion, was he replaced by somebody at the UNPROFOR headquarters as Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. I can't immediately think of the officer in question. I think he was a Frenchman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And even if General Nicolai was away from the headquarters, he was the Chief of Staff, and the other person, the Frenchman replacing him, was only there to take care of the daily business of the headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was acting as the Chief of Staff in the absence of Nicolai, in this case, who held that appointment, and he didn't stop holding that appointment while he was away.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Maybe you will not know the name of that Frenchman, that officer, but do you remember the position of that French officer who was acting for General Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd have to go and get the organogram of my headquarters to remember who it was. It isn't -- just to explain, because people changed over on a six-monthly basis, and they didn't all change at the same time, I have difficulty remembering who was where on what occasion during that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to your expert testimony. Please bear with me, as there may be things that I did not quite understand or things that I may not express very clearly. Yesterday, on page 70 of the transcript, you said that the Main Staff of an army is divided into various departments or branches, and you said that usually there is an operations sector, a logistics sector or branch, security, and so forth. Here is my question: The heads of those various branches, are they all assistant commanders?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they're not. They are chiefs of the branch or head of the department. They'll have a title something like that, or "Chief of Operations." They are members of the staff, as opposed to being assistant commanders or commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You were talking of an army in which those various branches or departments are branches of the staff sector; is that correct? The heads of those branches are not directly linked to the commander?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heads of the branches usually report to the Chief of Staff or the man fulfilling that function, and from there to the commander, or the commander, as if there's a hierarchy of commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What happens if an army is organised in such a manner that the head of the branch in charge of operation is subordinated to the Chief of Staff while the head of Logistics, Security, Personnel, are subordinated directly to the commander? In this particular example, would you also say that the heads of operations is at the same level of the other heads of the other branches who are subordinated directly to the commander?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could go back a bit and try and answer this question slightly more broadly. And I'm answering -- I'm still talking, as it were, to that expert statement as I remember it. The -- drawing a distinction between the commanders and the staff, that everybody is reporting ultimately to the commander and his immediate subordinate commanders, if they exist. The staff are there to support those commanders in their -- in discharging their responsibilities. The staff are usually organised, as I've described, into those branches of one description or another, and they are coordinated, and their work is brought to a single whole through the actions of the Chief of Staff, who is a very senior officer and can be a deputy commander in his own right. Then you have those who command. If you have, as we do in this case, assistant commanders, then the purpose of having those, if you like, extra commanders is to -- with their particular responsibilities, is to act as a focus on those particular issues, let's say logistics, and to make sure that the -- that the work of the headquarters, insofar as it affects that activity, is properly focused. You might see it if we looked at the corporate world of business that you would have a board of directors and you're each with separate responsibilities, but they are the directing hand of that corporation. That board of directors would be similar to but not precisely the same to the commanders within that construct that I have described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not want to interrupt the answer that the witness gave, and it's certainly not the witness's fault, but in my submission, understandably, he has strayed into the very area that the Chamber has said he must not stray into, because he has said, at line 25 of page 16: "If you have, as we do, in this case assistant commanders, then the purpose of having those ..." And he goes on and then gives the analogy with the corporate world. I objected when my learned friend for the Prosecution did it, and I object when my learned friend for General Miletic does it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau, you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry, this question did not deal with the Army of Republika Srpska. This was a general question which flows from the general answer given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let me confer with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, our response to your objection, Mr. Josse, is that we tend to agree with the statement of Madame Fauveau that the question was intended and was answered more within a generic background rather than with any specificity to the VRS, and in any case, we consider ourselves to be in a good position now, and even more later, to be able to make the necessary assessments. So let's proceed. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, would you agree that all armies do not have the same organisational and functional structure?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we say there was a difference between armies belonging to Western countries and armies which existed in the Warsaw Pact countries?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: In very broad terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The structure that you described yesterday is more based on the structure and functioning of a Western army; isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was trying to describe was in the expert statement, which is, I think, the one you're referring to. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that there were two broad models for how you might organise your staff. Neither are easily labelled "East" and "West." There is a tendency for those of the Warsaw Pact to be rather more to the centralised version I was describing in that expert statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said yesterday that in the system that you described, the Chief of Operations would have been primus inter pares. In this case, would it have been advisable to give the Chief of Operation to have the same rank of the other departments or even a higher grade? I'm not sure I was entirely clear, so let me repeat. If the heads of the other branches, Logistics, Security and others, are generals, in order to be the first among equals, do we need the Chief of Operations to be a general as well?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I'm using the phrase "first amongst equals" to describe that there isn't this obvious and clear rank structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But when you said that there wasn't an obvious and clear rank structure, you were talking about the structure that you described yesterday, this general structure that's a Western world structure?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm -- what I was trying to describe, both yesterday and in the expert statement, was the generic models of possible -- you know, the way staffs can work. The -- I don't think I've put a rank on anybody's appointment. I'm talking about the appointments people might hold and the function that they might be performing. The staff system is such runs through a whole army. It isn't just at one headquarters. You can -- the Chief of Staff of a brigade is a chief of staff. He doesn't have to have the same rank as the Chief of Staff of a division, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I am sorry, I think it is my mistake. I wasn't very clear. I'm talking about the Chief of Staff only, the Chief of Staff of a particular army. Within that Chief of Staff, you said that there were different heads of different branches, Logistics, Security and Operations, and you said that the head or Chief of Operations is first among equals. Within the Chief of Staff and only within the -- the Staff, sorry, among those various heads of branches, so that the Chief of Operations is -- can be first among equals, wouldn't it be necessary for him to have at least the same rank as the other officers?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think it is necessary, because it is the function he's performing rather than the rank he's holding.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And to assign somebody to an important function, it wouldn't be normal to assign to that particular function somebody with a high rank?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly in war, rank isn't necessarily the definition of competence, and you are just as likely to look for the right man for the job as you are for the right rank for the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: For a long time, you were an officer in the British Army. You were in many wars. Is it correct that you always respected the rules of engagement?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I always respected the orders I was given.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: There must have been an interpretation problem. My question dealt with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so, Ms. Fauveau, because the witness would have heard what we heard. Your question to him is whether he always respected the rules of engagement. If that was not the question, then you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, it was my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I meant was that if -- whether or not he always respected the law of war.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have always respected the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So, in any case, you think you were never in breach of them or you would never have deliberately breached a law of war?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think I have deliberately breached a law of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You were talking about a meeting you had on the 17th of September, 1995, with General Miletic. And I would like the witness to be shown evidence, P2908. Could we go to page 3 of this document. General, this is a document that was shown to you yesterday. It's about this meeting in September, where you spoke about Sarajevo and the modalities of the surrender of weapons around Sarajevo. Is it correct that it was the first time that you met General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is correct. I think that's the first time I met him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On paragraph 8 of this document, it is said [in English]: "General Miletic, an intelligent interlocutor, a man to do business with." [Interpretation] On the basis of this paragraph, is it fair to say that General Miletic made a good impression -- a positive impression on you?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 26 of the transcript, the Prosecutor asked you if you were surprised to see the Chief of Operations taking part in this meeting in Sarajevo, and your answer was: [in English]: "No, not at all, and he -- I had understood him to be there as the Chief of Staff. He was more than the Chief of Operations now. He was acting as the Chief of Staff of that headquarters." [Interpretation] When you said "he was more than the Chief of Operations now, he was acting as Chief of Staff of that headquarters," did you have in mind that meeting in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Was it only in September 1995 that you had the opportunity to meet General Miletic, who represented the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the time in September 1995, General Mladic and his Chief of Staff, General Ivanovic, and other people close to -- other officers close to General Miletic, were in Western Bosnia? I think there's been a mistake. There's first General Mladic and then his Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, and then another officer close to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Four lines in the transcript on page 22 should eventually be corrected. I'm just drawing the attention of whoever is responsible to make sure that those four lines are corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe the easiest way is for me to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that in September 1995, General Mladic, commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, his Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, and other officers close to General Mladic were in Western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that's correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene, Mr. President, just to clarify, cut off any further confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I -- one moment, because it's getting -- probably since I know your language, I was inadvertently following you in French, only to realise that now the rest is being also translated into French while we are on the English channel. So I think that's already fixed, so otherwise I would receive the translation of what I am saying, myself, in French. So Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just in hopes that it won't be repeated, I think there's an error at page 23, line 4, where General Mladic is referred to as the commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I just -- I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sorry, I meant the Army of Republika Srpska, and I apologise for this because I think it was my mistake and not the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. So are you still there, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not -- I'm still not entirely clear what the question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps you can -- the question is whether it's correct that in September -- I understand that Madame Fauveau hasn't specified which part of September -- General Mladic, the commander of the VRS, his Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, and other officers close to General Mladic were in Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's correct. I believe -- my memory is that's what I thought was the case, that his main effort was over on that side of the -- of Bosnia and those officers were over there with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that applies to the entire month of September or to any specific --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly up to the point of this meeting in -- whenever it is. I've forgotten the date now. The second half of September, anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 60 of the transcript, you said that for a long time your understanding was that the Chief of Staff was the general based in Banja Luka. Do you agree that this general in Banja Luka was General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is who I thought it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you prepared for your testimony on the 30th of October, you said to a representative of the OTP that the Chief of Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska was General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the particular conversation, but if there's a record of it, then that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit 5D515. It's a report of that meeting that you had with the representative of the OTP, and I'd like you to have a look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the middle of that paragraph, I'd like you to read a short sentence. [In English]: "General Milosevic being one of Mladic's chief of staff is clearly an error, as Mladic's chief of staff was General Milovanovic."

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to comment on that? Yes, it is a mistake in the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all, no, but I'd like to ask you a question. In your book, you refer to one of Mladic's chiefs of staff. Did you have the feeling that there were -- there were several chiefs of staff? In your dealings with army representatives, did you have the feeling that there were more than one chief of staff in the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certainly other chiefs of staff in other headquarters, but I think you're referring to the main headquarters, the -- Mladic's headquarters. The other -- Miletic, at this meeting, is an example of someone acting as a chief of staff when the Chief of Staff is elsewhere. I know we had other cases when Milovanovic was in Banja Luka. Then my understanding was that the Chief of Ops., who I understood was General Miletic, was acting as the Chief of Staff in the absence, if I can call it this, the real Chief of Staff, and that's what I'm referring to when I'm talking about there being one of his chiefs of staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 65 of the transcript, you said that you were not sure how you managed to know that General Miletic represented the Chief of Staff. Is it true that in your proofing session and last year, when you prepared your expert statement, you had the opportunity to look at many documents from the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, in the -- I don't think I saw documents in the proofing session in October. I certainly saw Bosnian Serb Army documents in -- before doing the expert statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And one of these documents was the documents where General Miletic's name was mentioned, and he was referred to as representing the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And would you say that it is on the basis of these documents that you concluded that General Miletic was the Chief of Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't been saying that. I've been saying he was standing in as the Chief of Staff. And while I have seen those documents, it was of interest to me, in my headquarters, to understand how the Bosnian Serb Army was working during 1995, and we would be asking questions whenever we had an opportunity of who was filling what job and what they were doing. It mattered to us to understand. And I had certainly had some understanding of the organisation and who was filling what job long before I saw those documents. What I can't tell you is just how much I knew before I saw those documents and how much I'd forgotten and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 65 of the transcript, and I'm talking about UNPROFOR in general, and you said that you were not always very well informed about the control and command in the Army of the Republika Srpska. Could you say whether the description of the functions of the Army of the Republika Srpska were always accurate in UN documents or sometimes were they not very reliable?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not informed, no, and as I say, we set out to find out. We were looking for the information. And I'm quite prepared to discover that there's inaccuracies in UN documents at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown page 5D468. It is a UN memorandum, a United Nations Protection Force memorandum, dated the 27th of July, 1995. Can the General be shown the very last box of this page, at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the middle of this box, you see that there is a description "BSA COS General Tolimir," so this abbreviation, "BSA COS," stands for Chief of Staff in the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would read that as such, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in July 1995, was General Tolimir the Chief of Staff in the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. And if you could take me back to the top of the document, we might see who sent -- who originated the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can we see the top of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can see it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Sector Sarajevo, and they are probably reporting what's being reported to them by the Ukrainian Detachment. If we slide down the -- keep going -- who's reported it, Ukrainian Company from Zepa. That doesn't surprise me, that they don't know the difference between an assistant commander and a chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP in August 1996, on page 6, third paragraph -- I don't think it's necessary to show it in e-court, but you said that General Tolimir was in the Army of the Republika Srpska, in charge of security, and that he was Mladic's main officer for political and military matters. It is Exhibit 6D180, if you'd like it to be shown to you. Can we go to page 6, third paragraph. And you see at the third sentence -- in fact, it's the third line. I don't know if it's the third sentence as well. [In English]: "We assessed Tolimir to be Mladic's principal staff officer on political military matters."

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown page 3 of the same statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You talked about General Hajrulahovic, Hajrulahovic, so it's the next-to-last paragraph on this page, and in this paragraph you said [in English]: " ... nicknamed 'Talijan' was a senior staff officer in the Bosnian Army and effectively number two in the military chain with specific responsibility for intelligence. [Interpretation] So General Hajrulahovic was not the Chief of Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't understand him to be so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Neither was he the Chief of Operations of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't think he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: However, he was effectively number two in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or at least that was your understanding of his position?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me understand better what is correct, General and Madame Fauveau. As I read it here, General Hajrulahovic, nicknamed Talijan, was a senior staff officer in the Bosnian army and effectively number two in the military chain with special responsibility for intelligence. So you're placing him in the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia -- of the BiH Army, of the armija, or are you restricting your assessment in relation to this section dealing with intelligence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's directed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. I'm not placing him -- they weren't organised in the same way, as I understood it and saw it, as the Bosnian Serb Army. The -- and what I'm trying to explain in this paragraph is that this man, which I can't pronounce his name either, so we'll call him "Talijan," was a -- had this position as being effectively number two in the military chain of command, with a special responsibility for intelligence. I can't divide the two out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Thank you. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So you just said that the armija and the VRS didn't have the same organisation, so is that correct that it is quite possible that there are significant differences in the importance of different positions in the two armies?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's probably fairer to say this is coloured by the personalities holding the positions, rather than the positions as they stood in some organisational chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let's go back to the meeting on the 17th of September, 1995. You said that the situation had changed and the Serbs became more cooperative. In the situation, they decided to send an officer who was more cooperating than the others?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I did say that. Can I see the document again?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So it was in the transcript. It's not what you said. You said that the situation had changed, and you said that the -- and the Army of the Republika Srpska cooperated in a better way, so I'm going to try and find the right page in the transcript. Your Honour, maybe we could take the break now. It will give me time to find the relevant page in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure, Madame Fauveau. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, we were talking before the break of what you said yesterday. I'm now in a position to show you page 70 of yesterday's transcript. Line 9 to 11, you're talking about the September meeting, and this is what you said about the representative of the VRS [in English]: "They were being at that stage and here presenting this a great deal more cooperative and focused than I had found the headquarters and these representatives before. [Interpretation] This is my question: General Mladic or the representative of the VRS decided to send General Miletic in a meeting where you were going to be as well, in a spirit of cooperation?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I found them. Whether that was the motivation of those who tempt them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, when the relationship with the Army of Republika Srpska were difficult, in particular in May, June and July, General Miletic never took place of any meeting with you; right?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in August 1996, you did not mention General Miletic when you talked about the various officers of the Army of the Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without scanning the document, I can't confirm that, but I'm pretty certain I didn't mention him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: One or two questions on the expert statement you gave. Would you agree that the organisation of Western armies could be described as functional?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: In contrast to what?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: To the organisation in countries of the former Soviet Union, i.e., countries of the Soviet Bloc which were more organised in a linear fashion.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the difference that you're trying to draw.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were on leave, it was General Gobillard, wasn't it, who was commanding the Sarajevo Sector, who was actually replacing you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was standing in for me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why wasn't it your Chief of Staff, General Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was a -- another commander on hand, in this case General Gobillard, and, secondly, because this was a multinational force and one of the major contributing nations to this force was France, and so it was appropriate that it was one of their officers that was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If for one reason or the other, General Gobillard could not take up that position while you were away, who would have commanded the UNPROFOR forces in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall us considering that eventuality. We made it sure that one or other of us was always in the -- in Sarajevo. I don't think we thought that through any further than we needed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, you spoke about Zepa, and you said that when you arrived in Zepa at the end of July 1995, you saw farms burning. This is on page 26 of yesterday's transcript. I'd like to show you document 6D29. It is a memorandum from Mr. Harland, dated 26th of July, 1995. According to the first paragraph of this memorandum, this document was drafted on the basis of a report from Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter. Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter was your military adviser; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the paragraph beginning with (ii), can you see the last sentence of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [In English]: "Many houses in the hills were burning, apparently torched by departing Bosnians"?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter, the Bosnians had set fire to the houses?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what he says. He says it's apparently torched by them, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that the additional forces of UNPROFOR were deployed in Zepa during the evacuation of the civil population?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this day in question or later on? I can't be sure of the dates, but we did deploy extra forces into the pocket, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 2 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, take a look at the second paragraph of the second page. Here it says that there are about 150 additional troops, but it means probably "additional men," and they came to reinforce the 79 Ukrainians. These extra forces were Frenchmen; isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if those are the ones that we deployed, they would have been French, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And those troops did arrive in Zepa, they did reach the enclave; right?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And they were not prevented to arrive by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In that paragraph, the following is said [in English]: "In addition, UNPROFOR Civil Affairs, a JCO team, and 2ICRC teams were in the pocket. UNPROFOR was actively assisting in the evacuation effort. UNHCR was not present in the pocket." [Interpretation] Would you agree, General, that these representatives of UNPROFOR Civil Affairs did reach Zepa?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And then again the Serbs did not prevent them from coming?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: There were also Red Cross representatives. They did reach Zepa as well?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they did, yes, and it says there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to that document, the representative of UNHCR did not go to Zepa. Is it fair to say that UNHCR representatives did not want to go there? They were allowed to, they were authorised to go by the Serbs, but they did not want to?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the case with any certainty, but I am -- would agree with you that if they had travelled there, they would have been able to get there, along with all those other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: To confirm what you've just said, I would like to show you documents 5D478. While we're waiting for this document to be displayed, this is an order from President Karadzic. It is an order of the 26th of July, 1995, by President Karadzic. I'd like paragraph 1 to be shown to the witness, please. It is an authorisation given to the UNHCR to go to Zepa. Could you please confirm that paragraph 1 of this document indeed gives authorisation to the UNHCR to go to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This order comes from President Karadzic. Yesterday and the day before yesterday, you spoke about the involvement of the Staff in the granting of authorisation for convoys to go to the enclaves, humanitarian and the UNPROFOR, but isn't it true that politicians as well as the political authorities were also involved in that process of authorisation? And here I'm talking about humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand -- are you wanting me to confirm what was going on inside Republika Srpska or with whom we dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Maybe I could refer you back to the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, to make things a bit more simple. It is Exhibit 6D180, your own statement. I'd like to see page 5 of that statement, please, first paragraph. Somewhere in the middle of this paragraph -- in this paragraph, you mention Nicolai Koljevic, and somewhere in the middle you say [in English]: "Although an important figure, did not have any authority or influence over Karadzic. His role was largely directed towards humanitarian issues. However, he played a significant role in the matter of the Sarajevo Airport and its closure to humanitarian flights and the clearance of UNHCR convoys to the Eastern Enclaves." [Interpretation] Do you remember that some politicians, and in particular Nicolai Koljevic, had indeed a significant role to play in this clearing process, the clearing of humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly agree that we dealt with them on this matter, yes, and indeed so did politicians on our side, if that's the correct name for them, like Mr. Bilton and Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let's now talk about the evacuation of the civilian population from Zepa. The extra forces that you deployed, the members of that French unit and the representative of Civil Affairs, were in the village of Zepa, among the civilian population, during the evacuation process; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in the early stages, they were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And while they were there, they never reported any irregularities during the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, and we addressed some of them. And there were -- there's at least one occasion when men were taken off a bus. I'd have to go back into the documents to find the case -- the details of the case. And we would represent these irregularities when they occurred, represent them to the -- General Tolimir and Co. at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. About this particular incident when men were taken off a bus, isn't it correct that it was the last convoy leaving Zepa?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details of it. I can recall that we had such an incident, but I don't remember the timing of it at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look at an excerpt of Exhibit 5D491, NIOD report. While we're waiting for this document to be shown to you, could you please confirm that you gave a statement to NIOD?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who are NIOD.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It is the Dutch institute.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was over the -- that was investigating Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Indeed, but it is not the parliamentary commission. This is something else.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I may have confused the two commissions, but I'm sure I gave this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: No, this is not your report. It is the report by the Dutch institute. My question is that: Did you give an interview to that institute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he did -- if you know that he did, why don't you present him with the interview or the relevant part on which you would like to -- if he did, because I don't know if he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, NIOD did not agree to give us that report. We don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the bottom of this page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the next-to-last paragraph, this NIOD report reads as follows [in English]: "Strictly speaking, Zepa did not fall. The Bosnian Serbs did not capture the enclave in the way they had overrun Srebrenica. Rather, it was abandoned by the Bosnian Muslim military forces and the population after which the latter made their way as displaced persons to Tuzla via Kladanj." [Interpretation] Would you agree that, in a way, Zepa was abandoned by the military forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. They were still fighting in the area. They didn't abandon it in the sense I understand you've asked the question. If by that you mean that they, in most cases, went over the Drina into Serbia, yes, they did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: That was at a later stage, but when the evacuation took place, there were no ABiH troops in the enclave -- not in the enclave but in the village of Zepa, where the civilian population was?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had -- they were not in the village, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that in the war which took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina, while you were there in 1995, and I will limit myself to that particular point in time, you saw a lot of movements of populations?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw some.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The same applies to Croatia. When the Croatian forces took Eastern Slavonia in May 1995 the Serb population left that particular area and mostly took refuge in Bosnia, in the territory held by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when the Serbs entered Srebrenica, the Muslim population left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And that same scenario happened again in Zepa; you? You could see it yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the population left.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And later on, when the Croat and Bosnian forces took villages and towns in the southeast of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serb population also left that particular place; right?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the southeast or --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Southwest, southwest.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was population movement there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The Serb population also left the Croat Krajina when the Croatian forces entered that area?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And even after the Dayton Agreements, when part of the city of Sarajevo where Serbs used to live was allotted to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serbs living in that particular part of Sarajevo left their dwellings?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you'll find that happened after my time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was common that when an army captured a particular village, that the population belonging to the other ethnic group, whose representatives did not hold power anymore, that these part of the population would leave the area?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Speaking about Zepa, men of military age, members of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zepa, they never surrendered to the Serbs, did they?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying that all men of military age were members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Not yet. But before answering my question, maybe you could tell me what your opinion was on that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I'm very happy to answer your question, but I wanted to understand the question I was being asked, and you are putting two things together which I wasn't convinced is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said, if I'm not mistaken, the day before yesterday that on Serb territory, all men of military age were members of the Serb military forces.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under conscription arrangements, that had been the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Didn't the same situation prevail in the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I don't believe that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Are you aware that in June 1995, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina proclaimed mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that occurring.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I may have made a mistake. This is the mobilisation order which predates your arrival, actually. It was in June 1992, but it was never revoked.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then so be it. I don't have any memory of that particular declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you do know that in the former JNA, there was a concept of territorial defence?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And within that framework, every man of military age was indeed a military man or was to become a military man, if need be?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was also based on that concept of territorial defence?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't necessarily based on it, but it had originated from it, yes. If I can make one -- only one other point, it isn't so much the manpower, it's their weapons in these circumstances. And while, of course, all those men had the potential to be a soldier, they didn't necessarily have the capacity to be one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, I think things are clearer now. About Zepa and about military forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were at Zepa before the fall of the enclave, members of those forces never surrendered to the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And according to your understanding, the Serbs didn't undertake major fighting against members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who took refuge in the hills?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to go back when you took the office of -- took the office of UNPROFOR commander in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Before taking this position, did you have the opportunity to meet your predecessor, General Rose?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met General Rose.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did General Rose brief you about the most important problems prevailing in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you started your work there, did the different commanders in your staff tell you about the problems in Srebrenica or problems relating to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have been briefed about Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And did you have the opportunity to talk to the Northeast Sector? I think this is the sector to which Srebrenica belonged, and did they tell you about the particular problems pertaining to the enclave, including problems between different political and military Muslim factions?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the detail of the briefings, but I did go to Sector Northeast and they would have briefed me about the whole of their area, which would have included Srebrenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to tell you about a report, and I apologise to you and to the Judges because I don't have the translation into English of this document. This is document 5D509. Witness, it is a report from the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina pertaining to the meeting that the representative of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had with Mr. Ken Biser. In this document, he's referred to as being the head of Civil Affairs of UNPROFOR for Sector Northeast. So this is a document from before your time, one or two months before you arrived. It's dated the 9th of December, 1994. First of all, was Mr. Biser still in Bosnia when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to talk to him about the situations in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know we had conversation and discussed the whole of his area, so we most certainly talked about Srebrenica as well. But the details of it, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On page 3 of this report, and I will read it to you in B/C/S and it will be translated into English, so a hypothesis has apparently been mentioned at this meeting, according to which: "They were holding them against their will in Srebrenica." I'm talking about the refugees: "The refugees were believing that they were being held against their will inside Srebrenica." When you arrived in Bosnia, you knew that there were many refugees in Srebrenica, people who arrived from villages around Srebrenica or other regions from Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Had you ever heard that this civilian population, these refugees, may have been prevented from exiting this area by the Srebrenica authorities, by the Muslim authorities?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- not in the way that you are describing it here. The way I'd seen it or observed it was in the early stages of the setting up of the enclave in Srebrenica, when at one stage in the very early stages there were some convoys that were taking people out, and at this point the government in Sarajevo began to object to UNHCR moving people out, and the government in Pale started to say that only convoys -- no empty vehicles could -- you know, you could have a convoy to go into Srebrenica, provided it came out with -- once it had dumped its humanitarian stores, it carried refugees out, and at that point it became an impasse. That's my memory of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So according to this document from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- and by the way, could we scroll up to the bottom of the page, and we could read the following [in English]: "Asked that particular question about the relationship between the government, the army and the police in Srebrenica." Can we go to the next page. I will read you what the commander of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina apparently told Mr. Biser and what he asked him. Apparently, they mention the following problems: "The over-population is the biggest problem. Two or three rows of three-storey houses for accommodation have been built, but people cannot move in without paying rent. There are empty houses already for weeks. The municipality did not allow people moving in. Power struggle, police. They want a share in the humanitarian aid. Municipal organs control the distribution of aid. Military elements control the municipality. There is animosity between the MUP chief and Naser Oric." Then, further down: "The military structures, Naser Oric and Zulfo Tursunovic, the commander of the 251st Brigade, are in conflict. The material interests are behind the conflict. Destruction of competition, different streams, involvement in crime, and smuggling on both sides. Nobody can leave Srebrenica to testify about the situation there. UNPROFOR is powerless and they can't do anything about that. The head of the police is complaining that the police does not have any authority over army members in preventing crime." I think I have read enough. So the meeting took place on the 9th of December, 1994. That was about one and a half months before you arrived. Had you ever been told about this concern by the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, relating to the situation in Srebrenica, including the conflict between the political and military authorities?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not been told of anything in that detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document. It's also a document written by the commander of the 2nd Corps. I'm sorry, it's just one sentence. It hasn't been translated into English. The document has nothing to do with your time in Bosnia, because it's dated the 5th of July, 1993, but what I think is interesting about this document -- so it's document 5D496, and can we show paragraph 5, as I said. It's a document written by the commander of the 2nd Corps at the time in 1993, and the last sentence of paragraph 5, he writes: "Under no circumstances allow any of the citizens to leave the demilitarised area." Can you tell us why it was important for the Bosnian Army to prevent the evacuation of the population of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know what they were thinking in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: From a strictly humanitarian point of view, wasn't it more logical to clear the evacuation of the population in that area? That was an overcrowded area.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there at the time, and I'm really not able to form an opinion as to the most sensible thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I fully accept your answer, but during your time in Bosnia in 1995, did you sometimes have the feeling that the Bosnian authorities were, in a way, holding the population hostages?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't understand it in that sense as holding the population hostage at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and when you started to work there, did you know that there were agreements signed between the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina relating to the demilitarisation of the areas of Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the documents such as I was shown, discussed the map of with General Mladic, yes, I had understood there had been those agreements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you document 5D503. It is the agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica. Can we show page 2 of this agreement. And can we go further down to see all the signatures. And go to the left. You'll see the date. So you see the agreement was signed on the 18th of April, 1993. It was signed by General Halilovic, General Ratko Mladic and Lieutenant-General Lars-Eric Wahlgren.
