I think I understood you to say between 1992 and 1994, you worked for the Ministry of Defence in the UK and you monitored the British missions and the operation within the Balkans, so this would have been what you would have worked on at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- that's the first time I think I've ever seen that document. The -- I could probably have seen it if I'd wanted to, in that it had been held in my headquarters in Sarajevo, but the British involvement in Srebrenica in 1993 was very limited, and that would have been the concern that I would be dealing with in -- when I was in London, in the Ministry of Defence. I wouldn't have been monitoring or trying to understand and second-guess the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I understand that your agreement was signed before you arrived, but theoretically, at least, this agreement was still in force when you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if I understood you correctly, no one told you about the existence of such an agreement.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I understood that an agreement existed. I didn't read it. If I had wanted to read it, I dare say I could have done, but I -- I don't recall having it out in front of me and reading the documents from 1993, and I didn't see it when I was in London.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the first page of this document, and can we scroll up to paragraph 4 [in English]: "The demilitarisation of Srebrenica will be complete within 72 hours of the arrival of the UNPROFOR company in Srebrenica." [Interpretation] And then [in English]: "All weapons, ammunition, mines, explosives and combat supplies (except medicines) inside Srebrenica will be submitted/handed over to UNPROFOR under the supervision of three officers from each side with control carried out by UNPROFOR. No armed persons or unit, except UNPROFOR, will remain within the city once the demilitarisation process is complete. Responsibility for the demilitarisation process remains with UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] So in this agreement, i.e., the demilitarisation process is described, but it never took place, did it?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Weapons clearly remained being used in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And according to this agreement, the last sentence of paragraph 4, it is not only weapons that were to be handed over, but also all units and all armed forces except UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the penultimate sentence, not the last.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another agreement that was reached a few weeks later. It's Exhibit 5D502. This is an agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa concluded between Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic and General Sefer Halilovic on the 8th of May, 1993, in the presence of Lieutenant-General Philippe Morillon. Did you have the opportunity to see this particular agreement?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, no doubt there was the opportunity. I don't recall reading it how many years later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Article 3. It's on page 2. It's very similar to what there was in the agreement signed on the 18th of April, 1993. In this Article, it says [in English]: "Every military or paramilitary unit will have either to withdraw from the demilitarised zone or submit/hand over their weapons. Ammunition, mines, explosives and combat supplies in the demilitarised zone will be handed over/submitted to UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] I think you already said that it never took place, and indeed a unit of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was still there in 1995, when you arrived, it was still in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the -- there was a collection point, and I've -- I had inspected weapons that had been collected in the weapon collection point, so perhaps some of it had happened, but I quite agree that there were armed men still inside the enclave. Whether they were in the city or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: However, there were in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was some armed men in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we go to Article 5 and paragraphs 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The agreement also provided for the following [in English]: "Non-combatants who are in or who are willing to enter the demilitarised zone, except for members of UNPROFOR, are not permitted to have in their possession any weapons, ammunition or explosives. Weapons, ammunition and explosives in their possession shall be seized by UNPROFOR. "Combatants will not be allowed to enter or to be in the demilitarised zone." [Interpretation] Now, these terms were never enforced, respected, were they?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- I can't account for the period until I was there, but it was certainly they weren't seizing any weapons when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go back to page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I think you mentioned the meeting -- you mentioned a meeting with General Mladic, where he complained that the -- that the boundaries of the zone were not properly established. Can we scroll up to the bottom of the page to show Article 1. In paragraph 2, it is said [in English]: "The demilitarised areas will include the area within the current lines of conflict. The precise boundaries will be marked by the UNPROFOR commander on the ground after consultations." [Interpretation] General, I understand it happened long before you arrived in Bosnia, but in a way, you inherited the situation that was difficult, if not impossible. According to your understanding, the UNPROFOR commander at the time in 1993 never clearly established the boundaries of that area, did he?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I think there was an established set of boundaries. The disagreement -- there was disagreement about where they were, but there were boundaries that were established, all right. Otherwise, they wouldn't have their positions to put the OPs on. I'm talking of Srebrenica when I'm using the example of OPs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a document where those boundaries were clearly established?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen maps on which where everyone stood was drawn, and in the meeting I described it's -- General Mladic made it quite plain that he disagreed with where those lines were where people were standing, but I had understood where everyone was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Right, but are you aware of the existence of an UNPROFOR official document sent to the warring parties in which those boundaries had been clearly determined?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have -- I don't know if such a document exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Was your understanding that both enclaves, Zepa and Srebrenica, should be physically separated?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no understanding other than that they were separated. Whether they should have been or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at Article 2 of this agreement. In fact, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that Article 2 refers to Article 60 of the 1st Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions. Can you confirm that Article 2 referred to Article 60 of the 1st Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- so it is written.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that according to Article 60 of the Protocol, as is indicated in this agreement as well, all fighters, as well as weapons and mobile materiel, military materiel, should have been evacuated from a protected zone?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd want to see the Geneva Convention to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Okay, I'll come back to that later. In any case, would you agree that the fact that the Bosnian authorities never withdrew the military unit from the protected zone was a substantial breach of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't -- it's not what they've said they're going to do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to page 5 -- no, I'm sorry, to page 2, Article 5 of the agreement. It is the last paragraph of Article 5, and it says, clearly, that combatants will not be allowed to enter or to be in the demilitarised zone.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if we take a look at page 4 of that same document, we see that this document was signed by General Halilovic, who was representing the ABiH; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: However, those combatants remained in the protected zone, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combatants remained there, yes, or, rather, to rephrase that, in my time there were combatants there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the period you spent there, there was a clear breach of the agreement, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that when such substantial breach occurs within a protected zone, well, the zone loses the status of a protected zone?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that follows, and I don't think it follows when these disputes are supposed to be sorted out in the presence of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D505. And, once again, I have to apologise. The documents are in B/C/S only. This is a report coming from the 1st Corps of the ABiH on the demilitarisation of Zepa. In fact, it is the inspection of the demilitarisation plan of the Zepa area which took place on the 20th of May, 1993. The document dates back to the 21st of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At the time, based on this ABiH document, the representative of the UNPROFOR, Mr. Valenti, said the following under 1. This is paragraph (a). Number 1: "That articles 1, 2 and 5 of the agreement have been honoured to the full by UNPROFOR; that the Serb side complied with its obligations arising from the agreement in the following way: That our side did not comply with Article 3 and that UNPROFOR does not want a museum in Zepa to be established. When they say that, they imply the contents and the types of the weapons that were surrendered." In contrast to Srebrenica, according to point 4 of that document which relates to Zepa: "Both sides agreed with the boundaries of the demilitarised zone that UNPROFOR identified as containing eight check-points." According to this document, the UNPROFOR representative in May 1993 found that the Serbs had complied with their obligations arising from the agreement. I'm talking about Zepa here, of course.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so. I have -- I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to this document or according to what I read in this document, the Bosnian side had not complied with its obligation arising from the agreement on the demilitarisation of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so. Again, I can't -- I wasn't there and I can't read this document, and I don't know its provenance.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let's go back to the time you served as commander in 1995. You're in a position to say that a military unit was there, a military unit from the ABiH was there in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Bear with me a little longer, but I promise you this is the last document without the translation. This is document 5D506. It's a document by the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, sent to the Srebrenica Defence Command, Naser Oric. The document is dated 1st of June, 1993. In the next-to-last paragraph - maybe we could have it shown on the screen - the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic, asks Naser Oric, the commander of forces in Srebrenica, the following: "Carry out sabotage and assault actions in the depth of aggressor's territory; establish connections with the citizens of Zepa; logistical supplies must be war booty. The summer days are good for guerrilla fight. Attack Chetnik bases, individual and group motor vehicles on the roads which carry materiel and technical equipment and food for the Chetniks on the front line and similar things. All the missions have to be carried out in the strictest confidence, but they have to be very skillfully coordinated." I fully understand that you were not there at the time and that you cannot read the document for yourself, but such a request, sent to the commander of armed forces in Srebrenica, is a clear breach of the agreement on demilitarisation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know that apart from not demilitarising the demilitarised zone, the Bosnian authorities regularly supplied those protected zones with weapons?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I know that or what was your question? I didn't know it in the sense that I could see it going on or anything like that, but it must have been happening or I -- they couldn't have maintained those people in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show you document 4D5, and it is translated into English. It is the speech delivered by the commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Rasim Delic, in front of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina in July 1996; after the war, that is. I'd like to have page 3 of that document displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, in the middle of this paragraph, there's a reference to the delivery of technical equipment, which started in April 1994. It says "materiel and technical equipment," and there's also a reference to the fact that [in English]: " ... Without the compromising their status as protected demilitarised zones." [Interpretation] Can you see this in the middle of the paragraph that's in the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is "MTS"?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I believe it is explained between brackets, materiel and technical equipment. Further down, not the next paragraph but the one after, there's a reference to the groups who went on foot, taking some weapons, equipment and communications equipment in the autumn of 1994. Can you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Then in the same paragraph, there's a reference to helicopter flights being organised.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, take a look at the bottom of the page, at the paragraph starting with [in English]: "The flights ...": "The flights were much more difficult than those in 1993 because of the following: The reduced area of the free territory; strong anti-aircraft defence of the Serbian aggressor; NATO control of the airspace and no-fly zones for all aircraft." [Interpretation] Is it true that all flights of all aircraft of warring factions were forbidden above Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already answered that and given enough information on it, Ms. Fauveau, and we are beginning to wonder why you are spending all this time on these events when most of what you have covered is already in the list of adjudicated facts and also agreed facts. We're letting you go because --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. I'm not trying to show that weapons did reach the area. What I'm interested in is the following:

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How is it possible -- or, rather, did you know that there were such flights, helicopter flights?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there had been helicopter flights once I was in the theatre, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you take action to prevent this from happening?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was down to NATO to do, and they found it extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why did they find it extremely difficult? Was there a specific reason?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were technical reasons to the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the NATO representative inform you of such problems, technical problems, to --

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that they existed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you tell them, inform them, or was it your opinion that leaving those weapons to reach protected zones could lead to a deterioration between the -- to the relationship between UNPROFOR and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- we didn't necessarily know that there were weapons on those helicopters. It was the flights, and there were flights by all sides going on. It wasn't only into the -- those two safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You spoke about problems faced by the Army of Republika Srpska due to a shortage of manpower. Is it true that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was deliberately using the enclaves to attack the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer the question on behalf of the Bosnian Army. The enclaves existed, they were there, and operations were conducted in and from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And those military operations which were conducted in the enclaves, around the enclaves, and in particular from the enclaves, they were in breach of the agreements on demilitarisation, were they not?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- of that document you showed me, they are in breach of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you receive reports on violations committed by the Bosnian side, relating to combats led from the enclaves? Did you receive reports from the Dutch-Bat or from the Ukrainian Battalion on Zepa, reports indicating that such things were happening?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relevant sectors would have received the reports, and then they would have reached me, yes, or my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you ever think of taking stronger action against the Bosnian side to prevent such attacks from happening?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean "stronger action"?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You're right, indeed. Did you take any measures at all after you received such reports?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we had a particular case, we would pursue it, and in many cases these would be protested and so forth in much the same procedure as was carried out with -- to the Bosnian Serbs when other things happened from that side.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But on various cases, force was used against the Serbs. Did you ever think of using force against the Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no case where -- that I can recall in my time when the Bosnians attacked my forces, so I had no cause to use force in defence of myself or my forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it true that when you arrived -- a few days after you arrived, actually, the armed forces of Srebrenica took members of the Dutch-Bat hostage?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, an agreement on the cessation of hostilities was in force between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But, very quickly, you draw the conclusion that the agreement was not respected?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was very quickly, but fairly soon that became clear to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we still have five minutes left, but I'm about to show the witness another document, so maybe it is appropriate for us to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to have a break now, but it will be of 20 minutes' duration and not 25, but then we don't finish at 7.00, we finish five minutes or thereabouts before. Okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to show the witness another excerpt from the NIOD report. It is Exhibit 5D494. Can we go to page 3, the third paragraph from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, can you see the paragraph starting with: "In Akashi's opinion ..."? In this paragraph of this report, it is said -- the following is said, and to put things in perspective, what is at stake here is the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement that has been -- that began in 1995 [in English]: "In Akashi's opinion, everything was aimed at an ABiH offensive as soon as the weather conditions would improve. The Bosnian government had not explained the reasons for this obstruction against the arranged Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, but Akashi did have the impression that the Bosnian government wanted to make it clear to the International Community that the Cessation of Hostility Agreement had no effect, with the purpose of discrediting the Bosnian Serbs. However, in reality it was the Bosnian government that failed to fully comply with it. That put UNPROFOR in a deadlock. In addition, the Bosnian government used the relatively quiet period to financially squeeze the UNPROFOR for rent of facilities ..." [Interpretation] Do you agree with that opinion, with Mr. Akashi's view that the Bosnian government in fact failed to respect this Cessation of Hostilities Agreement?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear that that is Akashi's. This is their report of Mr. Akashi's views. But I would generally agree that the cessation of hostilities was going to end, and it was towards the end of March that the first full-scale attacks occurred by the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Bosnians took financial advantage of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It wasn't my side of the business at all. I have no idea as to who was paying the rents and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You were talking about supply problems the day before yesterday, about problems relating to supplying UN forces, and can we -- can we go back to this page? Can we go up on this page to the second paragraph in this report? And by the end of the paragraph, the following is said [in English]: "In addition, the ABiH imposed limitations upon the UNPROFOR freedom of movement, said Akashi. He also concluded that not only did the Bosnian Serbs impose restrictions on sending fuel supplies to UNPROFOR, but the Bosnian Muslims were doing the same, supplying the troops in the Sapna Thumb (where the Dutch-Bat company was stationed) and Srebrenica was hindered by the restrictions imposed by the ABiH." [Interpretation] Did you know that the Bosnians imposed restrictions on the -- on UNPROFOR's freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I don't actually remember the particular case that you've put there, that's put there in that paragraph. I cannot -- I can't confirm that happened. There were restrictions. They were nothing like as those imposed by the Bosnian Serbs. But we couldn't go wherever we wanted, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you another part of NIOD's report. It is 5D54. Can we go to page 3, page 3 of this document. Somewhere in the middle of paragraph 2, there's a sentence that starts as following, and it deals with the time of May or June 1995 [in English]: "Haukland pointed out in a letter of protest to the ABiH command in Sarajevo that this was one side of the coin. He complained about ABiH's limitation of UNPROFOR's freedom of movement and the curfew and the hostility experienced from ABiH soldiers. For this reason, he was no longer able to perform his operational and humanitarian duties satisfactorily. Haukland's anger could be explained: The ABiH (the 1st Corps in Visoko) blocked the flow of humanitarian goods to the Tuzla region, where 250.000 people were dependent on aid. Governor Izet Hadzic was not up in arms about this, although he did have concerns about the humanitarian situation in Srebrenica." [Interpretation] Had you heard of this incident?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's more than -- it's not -- the particular exchange of letters, I don't recall at all. That this was going on in June, I am well aware of, yes. Those are the sort of restrictions I was referring to when I said that the ABiH were doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just to clarify it, did you know that these people from Tuzla, these 250.000 people, were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they were all Muslim, but most would have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you know that there were particular problems in Srebrenica between members of the Dutch-Bat and members of the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that being brought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we go to page 4 of this document. It is right at the end of the page, the last paragraph [in English]: "At Yellow Bridge, the VRS, both on the outward and on the return journey, carefully checked the quantity of fuel in the vehicles' tanks. The VRS soldiers appeared friendly, but the convoy leader could not say that about Dutch-Bat: The Dutch-Bat soldiers were instructed to check the vehicles, which was done conscientiously. Furthermore, each truck was photographed. Major Franken explained this by saying that Dutch-Bat performed the checks as a precautionary measure, because otherwise the ABiH would do so; he feared that the ABiH would also set up a roadblock." [Interpretation] You said that you weren't aware of particular problems between the UNHCR and the Dutch-Bat, but did you hear or was it reported to you by Sector Northeast that Dutch-Bat was checking the convoys going into the zone?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but it doesn't surprise me that they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you Exhibit 5D490. And while we are waiting, I can tell you that this document is a summary of the meeting you had with Dr. Ganic on the 21st of June, 1995. In the first paragraph of this document, one can see that during this meeting, the freedom of movement was discussed, amongst other things, freedom of movement for UN convoys and UNPROFOR troops. Is this correct that this was the topic of this meeting with Dr. Ganic, that you talked about the freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could see the whole document, I might be able to confirm it, but it's -- certainly freedom of movement was an issue during that month.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in June 1995, freedom of movement was restricted by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was indeed a problem for UNPROFOR troops, so is this what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were having trouble moving around in Central Bosnia, and particularly in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And I'd like you to read the last sentence of paragraph 4. It's now General Hajrulahovic speaking, and he said the following: [In English] That his troops would always allow the UN freedom of movement, providing that UN gave 24 hours' prior notification. [Interpretation] This procedure of 24 hours' notification was a standard procedure that was applied by all parties, and by that I mean that the Serbs also asked you to give them 24 hours' notice?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the standard procedure as to whether this was -- from that, I read that this was a new request, rather than standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So you're telling us that you don't remember it to be a standard procedure, but would you say that there was a standard procedure for the identification of convoys?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The day before yesterday, on page 17477, the shortage of medicines in Srebrenica, were you aware that the Dutch-Bat supplied the local population with medicines?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly treated the local population on occasions. I didn't -- I don't recall whether or not they actually supplied medicines from their own supplies, but I know they treated them on some occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another part of the NIOD report. It is Exhibit 5D53. And can we go to page 2 of this report and zoom on paragraphs 2 and 3. I'm going to read you paragraph 2 and part of paragraph 3. According to this report, the following is said [in English]: "An estimated 90 per cent of all medical consumables were used in the treatment of the local population, and the remainder in the treatment of Dutch-Bat's own personnel. On arrival in the enclave, Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans regarded the stopping of support to the local population, or a reduction in this support, is a serious threat to his mission. He believed, moreover, that it would damage the good relations with the local administration and population that had been built up with such great care and effort. He urged the maintenance of medical aid at its existing level." [Interpretation] And then the next paragraph [in English]: "The Netherlands Armed Forces had no guidelines for the provision of aid to third parties. It was the UNPROFOR policy that, except in emergencies, the provision of medical aid was a matter for nongovernmental organisations and not for the military. The comment by General Rupert Smith when he took up his position as Commander of Bosnia and Herzegovina Command that the humanitarian aid would become one of the troops' main objectives thus merely sowed confusion, since he had no say in logistic matters." [Interpretation] Is that an accurate description of the situation as you knew it?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't understand -- if we take your first paragraph you read out that starts with: "An estimated 90 per cent ...," that paragraph, that's what I thought the Dutch-Bat was doing. The proportions, I didn't know, but supporting a local population with your surplus, by all means. Whether I was giving an order or a comment -- we're now in the second paragraph, I'm sorry -- the general policy of the UN, it wasn't so much UNPROFOR as I understand it or, rather, understood it, was that you didn't produce military units to support the local -- military medical units to support the local population if others were available. It was better that these things were done by civil medical facilities. The -- I would certainly have considered that Dutch-Bat, in its circumstances in Srebrenica, was in a situation equating to an emergency and it would be perfectly proper for it to support the local population. Whether I'm giving a comment or giving an order, I have no idea in that next sentence. And if it confused anyone, they had only to come and ask, and I don't recall anyone asking, nor do I consider I had no say in logistic matters. I don't agree with that, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that the situation regarding medical supplies improved in April, and later on there was no longer a medicine shortage in Srebrenica? And of course I'm talking about April 1995.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the situation improved after my visit, when that delivery of medical stores arrived. Whether it -- what happened after that, I don't say that that was -- went on being an improvement at all. Supplying Srebrenica remained a problem right to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown page 4. That is the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you see the third paragraph, starting with: "On 10th of April, 1995 ..." [in English]: "On 10 April 1995, the transport of medical supplies resumed, greatly improving the situation as regard the stock of these goods. There were hardly any more shortages at that moment; indeed, supplies of some articles were actually much too high. All worries about the level of medical supplies were completely resolved." Well, I think that's enough. Did you have a more specific knowledge on the situation regarding medicines or would you be ready to accept what's written in this report?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept what's written in this report as a description of what's happening to the Dutch Battalion, not to Srebrenica as a whole. This is -- as I understand this, this is saying that the Dutch are exhausting their supplies at the rate of 90 per cent to the -- in support of the civil population, and the resupplies bring them up to a satisfactory level and allows them to continue supporting the population at that rate. That isn't the same thing as saying that Srebrenica is properly supplied.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you continue reading the text where I stopped, you'll see the following [in English]: "In the reply to questions in Parliament, Minister of Defence Voorhoeve stated that the supplies were once again sufficient to permit medical care both for civilians and for the Dutch soldiers. Medical aid to the local population was indeed resumed at full capacity, with an average of two operations per day." [Interpretation] Would this change your opinion, and would you accept the position as regards medicines, would you accept the fact that the situation was quite satisfactory in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't accept it. This is about the Dutch Battalion, not about the population as a whole in Srebrenica. And, yes, they, the Dutch Battalion, now have their supplies and they're able to carry out the local -- support of the local population as it is -- as they were beforehand, but it is not saying that there is a satisfactory flow of supplies, as a whole, into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that during a war, living conditions are usually deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: For who?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: For the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm talking about ordinary people. I'm not talking about people with high political positions or military positions.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't -- a statement such as you've asked me to agree with, I can't agree with. No, I don't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And would you agree that the Republika Srpska, in particular, was under embargo, it was a total embargo; it was not only an embargo on weapons, but on everything else, every kind of supplies, apart from humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, yes, it was a difficult time for the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it fair to say, about the Republika Srpska, that living conditions of the Serb population or the population within the Republika Srpska as a whole were quite bad?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were not good.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember having given a declaration statement - you mentioned it a moment ago - to the Parliamentary Commission of the Netherlands which investigated the events in Srebrenica in 2002? I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D489. I'd like us to go to page 10 of this document, to the bottom of the page, last column. You're talking about life in the enclaves at the very end of that paragraph. It begins, actually, in the middle of the paragraph, and that's what you said [in English]: "We had been trying for the last couple of weeks of June to get supplies into Srebrenica, amongst other enclaves, and to do it by air again. These attempts were paying to pass the debate with Zagreb at the time. Zagreb had negotiated a number of convoys, as I recall it, through Serbia and into Belgrade's hand as it were into these enclaves. Life was bad and unpleasant and isolated and all those things, but it was not disastrous, it was not catastrophic." [Interpretation] Was that your assessment of the situation in Srebrenica then?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be my description, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When the Serbs took the enclave of Srebrenica, you heard, maybe not right away, but during the days after, you heard of the separation of men of combatting age, of military age?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at page 15 of this statement. It's at the very bottom of the page in the first column.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this last paragraph, you're talking about the separation of the males, and that's what you said [in English]: "Separation of the males from the females was the normative behaviour of the Serbs in those circumstances, or for that matter, the Bosnians in their circumstances had done that before. And so might the Dutch Army if you had arrived on a position and was sorting out who was who at the time."

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find this. What page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the first column --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm in the wrong column, that's right. I was in the wrong column. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want, I can give you some time to read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And does it go on?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can continue if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I read over to the top of the page? No, this other way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It continues as follows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the basis of this paragraph that you've just read, and on the basis of what you said at the time, can it be said that the separation of males, in itself, was something which could have been motivated by military reasons, that from a military point of view it could have been understood?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you page 5 of this statement. You were talking about the Serb forces and the general military situation in existence between the fall of Srebrenica. What I'm interested in is the last column, first paragraph of the last column. Take some time to read the whole column, if you want, but in fact what I'm interested in is what is in the middle of this column, where you said [in English]: "What they did need to do was to stop the Bosnian conducting operations from out of them. They needed to make sure that the UN acted to control the Bosnians and not let the Bosnians use the UN as a shield to their activities.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you located the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then your question, Madame Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the Serb military activities around the enclaves were necessary, from a military point of view, and justified, from a military point of view?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not prepared to argue for justification or not. I can certainly understand what they were doing. That's the whole point in my argument in -- with myself in this thesis, that this is what they would be doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you did understand the restrictions imposed on convoys going to the enclaves? I'm sorry, there may have been a mistake in the interpretation, but that may be my own mistake. Would it be fair to say that you also had an understanding for restrictions which may have been imposed to convoys who were supposed to go to the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's be quite clear. I, as, if you like, my own intelligence officer, can sit and try and put myself in another man's position and to try and understand what he's doing and why he's doing it. That doesn't make me agree with him or accept the rationale. Nevertheless, one tries, in understanding these things, to put yourself in the other person's shoes. That is what I'm doing in this thesis. That I was tendered to be proved right is neither here nor there. What I was explaining is what I was thinking the Serbs, in this case, were conducting themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like now to show you the report drafted on the basis of your interviews with the Office of the Prosecutor in November 2002. This is Exhibit 6D181. Can we go to page 4, please, fourth paragraph of page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said, during those interviews of November 2002, the following [in English]: "I thought to myself, what if I was Mladic. What would I do to shift the balance of forces to advantage of the Serbs? I would squeeze the enclaves, make them irrelevant, starve them." [Interpretation] Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just what I've been trying to explain to you, that I'm putting myself in Mladic's position.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that the attitude -- the conduct of Mladic was caused by a military necessity?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't jump to that conclusion either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps some time frame or context as opposed to the way the question is currently phrased, which is conduct of Mladic. I mean, it's awfully broad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can proceed, Mr. Thayer. I think the witness can handle it. He knows exactly what the question is about and what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you receive information about a meeting between the Dutch-Bat members and the military unit of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was in Srebrenica in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall receiving such information, but I dare say if such a meeting had occurred, it would have been reported.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D498. It is a document from the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated 30th of May, 1995. Could we show the first page of the English document to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the first paragraph on this page, it is said the following [in English]: "A meeting between delegations of military and civilian authorities in Srebrenica was held with the Srebrenica UNPROFOR Dutch Battalion representative." [Interpretation] And then further down in paragraph 3 [in English]: "The meeting commenced as scheduled and was attended by Major Franken, Battalion Deputy Commander, and Warrant Officer Rave on behalf of the UNPROFOR Command. At the beginning of the meeting, they told us they would be frank, to the point, that they wanted the meeting to be of the highest level of confidentiality, that they did not want any military observers to be present at the meeting, and that they would tell us why at the end of the meeting." [Interpretation] Did anyone tell you at any stage that the Dutch-Bat had secret meetings with members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secret from who?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Apparently from the observers.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. I don't recall any such thing, and I'm assuming that you're -- this document is referring to the UNMOs, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 2 of this document, page 2 of the English version. It's the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the middle of this first paragraph, in the upper part [in English]: "They have decided to defend themselves and given the situation the Major said ..." [Interpretation] Did you find this part of the document?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got a paragraph that starts: "They were to be attacked ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: That's the one, yes, somewhere in the middle, the eighth line from the top.

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It seems that the major, Major Franken, would have said in this meeting. [In English] "Little remains but to jointly defend the enclave. This is obvious," he said. [Interpretation] Let me repeat what I have just said, because it has not been recorded [in English]: "Little remains but to jointly defend the enclave. This is obvious." [Interpretation] I believe you said you didn't have any particular information on an attack against the enclave, but did you know or did you learn at a later stage that members of the Dutch-Bat had entered into talks with the ABiH as to the conduct that would be necessary should an attack take place?

utterances.speaker: Rupert Smith [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- this -- the account in this paragraph, I don't -- is news -- new to me, and I don't have any memory of anyone reporting such an event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau, we need to stop here. We will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and everybody have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
